notes.claim: Speed control and voltage control are two separate systems on a generator set: speed control shares kW and voltage control shares kVAr.
Turning the rotor makes a rotating magnetic field, which induces a three-phase voltage in the stator winding.
A three-phase alternator has three single-phase windings spaced so that the voltage in each phase is displaced by 120° from the other two.
The rotor speed fixes the frequency: a two-pole machine must turn at 3600 rpm to make 60 Hz.
The automatic voltage regulator controls the alternator output voltage by adjusting the exciter stator field strength.
A self-excited alternator will not maintain a short-circuit current; it decays quickly unless the fault is cleared at once.
A dedicated AVR supply lets the alternator sustain its output during a short circuit, so the load's protection devices have time to clear the fault (i2).
The synchroniser and load sharing work by adjusting the reference points of the governor and the AVR (i2, forward line).
Each phase is an internally generated voltage in series with a reactance, made of armature reactance and the coil's self-inductance, and a series resistance.
A lagging load needs a larger internal voltage than a leading load, so a larger field current is needed for the same terminal voltage.
Three-phase generator sets are rated for 0.8 power factor loads.
Only a slightly leading power factor can make a generator set lose voltage control.
Leading power factor comes from a lightly loaded UPS, high intensity discharge lighting and power factor correction capacitors.
Droop is the percentage change in speed that takes the governor through its full action.
With 5 percent droop, full-load speed is 100 percent and no-load speed is 105 percent.
A load step the engine cannot supply at once reduces the engine speed, which is a frequency dip.
Four electrical quantities of the incoming machine must match the running bus within tolerance before the breaker closes: voltage, frequency, phase sequence and phase angle.
An autosynchroniser sends the close command early, at an advance angle, to allow for the breaker's closing time.
A closure out of step can send a synchronising current larger than a three-phase fault at the generator.
Where to close by hand is contested: one practice closes as the pointer passes about 11 o'clock, another at about 5 minutes to 12, both turning slowly in the fast direction (i5).
notes.contested: Wikipedia closes at about 11 o'clock, slowly in the fast direction; the PSRC report closes at about 5 minutes to 12.

notes.claim: Synchronising windows are settings that differ by maker: one maker gives a voltage difference of 0.5%, a trade site gives voltage within about 5% and frequency within 0.1 to 0.5 Hz (i5).
Ashore, BS 7671 Section 551: interlocks and switching must make parallel operation of a standby set with the supply impossible (i5, one line).
The kW a set shares in parallel is a direct function of its engine's real power output.
Raising the fuel to one set in a paralleled group does not raise the speed or the frequency.
Raising the excitation of one paralleled set raises that set's share of the kVAr and lowers its power factor.
Paralleled sets need the same droop, falling in frequency at the same rate from no load to full load (i6).
A factory-fitted droop CT is preset for a 5% voltage drop at full load and zero power factor (i6).
Third harmonics add in the neutral and can drive large neutral currents between paralleled sets (i6).
A 2/3 pitch winding makes no third harmonics, so it suits paralleling (i6).
On an earthed scheme, one and only one running set's neutral is earthed at a time, to avoid circulating currents (i6).
Voltage (reactive) droop does not work well against the mains, because the mains voltage varies as its load changes (i6).
A set running alone has its droop CT shorted by a switch, for normal voltage regulation (i6).
When setting up sets to run in parallel, the voltage setting on one is trimmed last, to cancel the current circulating between them (i6).
A reverse power relay detects real power flowing into the generator, which happens when it loses its prime mover.
A loss of excitation during parallel operation causes circulating currents, pole-slipping and torque and current surges.
Decrement curves show an alternator's fault current through the sub-transient, transient and sustained periods of a fault.
A self-excited alternator's short-circuit current decays to nothing unless the fault is cleared quickly.
For i7: a reverse power relay gives a diesel anti-motoring protection, against the danger of explosion and fire from unburned fuel.
Starting current is typically six times a motor's full-load current and stays high until the motor reaches about 75 percent of rated speed.
When the load step is fast, the regulator cannot beat it, so the voltage drop equals that with no regulator present.
If the generator recovers motor voltage to at least 90 percent of rated, the motor develops 81 percent of rated torque.
Starting three 100 hp motors one after another, not together, cuts the starting kW needed by 40 percent.
When an engine slows under a load step, the frequency dip makes the alternator voltage dip worse.
After a blackout, a power management system starts the generators automatically (Blackout Recovery).
With dead bus synchronising, any number of generators can be online and in parallel within about 15 seconds.
